summaries.example: Imagine pointing at a dog and saying, “This dog is running.” The word “this” helps show which dog you mean. A name such as “Milo” can also pick out one animal. Medieval thinkers asked whether “Milo” and “this dog” work in exactly the same way.
summaries.summary: A singular term is a word or phrase that signifies one individual thing. Medieval scholars examined examples such as proper names, pronouns, and phrases like “this man.” They did not study the topic in one single book. Instead, they discussed it in grammar books, logic textbooks, philosophical commentaries, and theological writings. Their questions included: Do names have meaning as well as a referent? How are names different from pronouns? Can a name refer to someone who has died? What happens when a speaker points at the wrong thing? Some scholars treated names as connected with identifying features, while others emphasized direct reference to an individual. Peter Abelard offered an important early theory, and John Buridan later developed a broad account involving singular concepts, mental language, and different kinds of pointing. The disagreements show how a small word such as “this” can raise large questions about language and thought.
key_ideas: Medieval thinkers studied names and pointing words as part of grammar, logic, philosophy, and theology.
They asked whether a proper name has meaning in addition to pointing to one thing.
They wondered how we can talk about someone who lived long ago or someone who does not exist.
Different thinkers gave different answers about names, descriptions, and pronouns.
John Buridan developed one of the fullest medieval accounts of singular terms.
summaries.why_it_matters: We use names and pointing words every day, but we often assume they are simple. Medieval thinkers showed that they involve questions about meaning, memory, truth, and identity. Their discussions also help explain how language can talk about people who are absent, past, or only imagined. Studying these ideas teaches us to look carefully at what our words do.

important_terms.definition: A word or phrase meant to point to exactly one individual thing, such as a name or “this dog.”
A name given to one particular person, animal, or thing, such as “Socrates.”
A word such as “this” that helps point to something, usually something present.
What a word or phrase picks out or stands for.

questions_to_think_about: Does a name still work after the person who had it dies?
What must you know in your mind before “this one” can point successfully?
Can one phrase point to different things on different occasions?

summaries.example: Suppose a historian says, “Aristotle was a philosopher,” while never having met him. Buridan’s theory raises a question: does “Aristotle” function here as a genuinely singular term, or does the speaker use a description built from information such as “a Greek philosopher”? The answer depends partly on how the name was connected to an original act of naming and what concept the present speaker possesses.
summaries.summary: Medieval theories of singular terms investigate how language identifies individual things. The central examples are proper names such as “Socrates,” demonstratives such as “this one,” and compounds such as “this man.” The topic developed through interaction among grammar, Aristotelian and Porphyrian logic, philosophical theories of individuation, and theology. A recurring issue was whether proper names signify only an individual or also an identifying quality or concept. If a name signifies a bundle of accidental features, it may seem connotative rather than a simple term of substance. If it signifies only its bearer, however, one must explain how it supports essential predication and logical inference. Another issue concerns names whose bearers are absent or deceased. Medieval authors proposed different relations among a word’s signification, its suppositum, the thing it appellates, and the concepts in the speaker’s mind. Demonstratives introduce further complications because their successful use normally depends on an act of pointing and an identifiable object. Abelard’s twelfth-century account sharply separated naming from signifying and treated “Socrates” and “this man” as logically equivalent in an important respect. In the fourteenth century, Buridan gave a more systematic theory. He described “this man” as a vague individual, discussed determinate singular concepts, and allowed some uses of names and pronouns beyond immediate physical presence. His account also explored how names can remain stable through time and how later speakers may use names connected to an earlier naming act.
key_ideas: The medieval category of singular terms included proper names, demonstratives, and combinations such as “this man,” but their semantic structures were disputed.

Grammar often associated proper names with a substance and an identifying quality, whereas logic required an account of how a singular term could signify an individual without becoming merely descriptive.
Questions about empty or past names—such as names of deceased individuals or not-yet-existing individuals—made the relation between signification, thought, and existence especially difficult.
Medieval logicians connected singular terms with syllogistic inference, descent from universal claims to singular claims, and the theory of supposition.
Peter Abelard distinguished naming from signifying and argued that “Socrates” and “this man” could have the same logical meaning while differing grammatically.
John Buridan distinguished vague individuals, determinate individuals, demonstrative concepts, and extended uses of names, producing one of the most comprehensive medieval theories.
summaries.why_it_matters: The subject connects ordinary language with major philosophical problems: how words mean, how thoughts represent individuals, how propositions can be true about the past, and how logical conclusions depend on reference. It also shows that disputes about names are not merely grammatical. They affect theories of knowledge, identity, existence, and religious language. Medieval analyses anticipate later questions about descriptions, empty names, direct reference, and the relation between public words and private concepts, while remaining grounded in their own logical and theological frameworks.

important_terms.definition: A term that signifies one individual, including proper names, demonstratives, and phrases such as “this man.”
The individual or thing for which an expression stands in a particular linguistic use.
An expression whose interpretation depends on an act of indicating, such as “this one.”
A mental representation or act associated with a spoken expression in theories of mental language.
A theory of terms concerned with what they stand for in propositions and inferences.
A term that does not add a connotation of properties outside what it signifies; medieval authors called such terms absolute or non-connotative.
A term used for different things because each particular use is tied to a different act or concept.

questions_to_think_about: Can a proper name refer directly while still having some kind of sense?
If “this man” is used while pointing at a stone, is the resulting statement false, meaningless, or otherwise defective?
Should a true universal proposition license a singular conclusion when the singular individual no longer exists?
If two people are named “John” for the same reason, does that make the name univocal?
Does a causal connection to an original naming event help explain how later speakers use a proper name?

summaries.example: At school, one student might say, “This player scored,” while pointing to a teammate. Later, someone might say, “Jordan scored,” even when Jordan is not in the room. The first expression depends strongly on pointing at the right person. The second seems to depend on a name and on shared knowledge. Medieval thinkers asked whether these two expressions have different kinds of meaning and whether either one can work when the person is absent.
summaries.summary: The entry studies medieval ideas about singular terms: expressions intended to signify one individual. Examples include proper names, demonstrative pronouns, and phrases such as “this man.” Medieval scholars drew on grammar, logic, philosophy, and theology rather than writing one separate subject textbook. They asked whether a proper name has a sense as well as a referent, whether names and pronouns work alike, and how a name can refer to someone who is absent or dead. They also considered expressions that do not successfully refer, such as a demonstrative used while pointing at nothing or at a stone when the speaker says “this man.” In logic, singular terms created problems for syllogisms and for reasoning from a general statement to claims about particular individuals. Some thinkers regarded proper names as temporary terms whose signification depended on the continued existence of the bearer. Others argued that language and thought can preserve reference after the bearer is gone. Peter Abelard made a major distinction between naming a thing and signifying a quality or nature. John Buridan later developed a detailed theory of singular concepts and distinguished different ways an individual can be known, including as “this man” and as a fully identified person. The entry follows these debates from ancient sources through medieval developments and later influence.
key_ideas: Medieval scholars treated names and demonstratives as both grammar topics and logic topics.
They disagreed about whether proper names carry descriptions or qualities, or mainly identify an individual.
Pointing words can fail if nothing is pointed to or if the pointed-at object is the wrong kind of thing.
Names create puzzles when their owners are dead, not yet alive, or only imagined.
The topic affected arguments, syllogisms, and claims about what words can stand for.
Abelard and Buridan offered especially important accounts, though their solutions were not identical.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate matters because identifying one thing is central to speaking truthfully and reasoning correctly. A name seems simple, but it raises questions about memory, knowledge, identity, and existence. Medieval discussions also show how grammar and logic can influence each other: the way a word behaves in a sentence may affect how thinkers understand the thing it represents. These issues remain useful whenever we ask what a name means or how we can talk about people and things that are not present.

important_terms.definition: A word or phrase that picks out one individual thing rather than a group or kind.
A name used for one particular individual, such as “Socrates.”
A word like “this” or “that” whose use normally involves pointing or identifying something.
The thing a word or phrase refers to in a sentence.
A way of analyzing what a term stands for in a statement or argument.
A word that can have different meanings or referents in different uses.

questions_to_think_about: Would “this student” still refer successfully if the student left the room?
Can a name keep its meaning after its bearer dies?
Is a phrase like “the first person to reach the North Pole” a singular term even if it contains general words?
Why might two people using “this man” be understood as making different uses of the same phrase?
Can a word refer to one thing even when the speaker knows only a description of it?
